<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We use the Almkvist–Zeilberger algorithm, combined with a weighted version of the Even–Gillis Laguerre integral due to Foata and Zeilberger, in order to efficiently compute weight enumerators of multiset derangements according to the number of cycles. The present paper is inspired by important previous work by Mourad Ismail and his collaborators, done in the late 1970s, but still useful after all these years.</jats:p>
title: Efficient weighted counting of multiset derangements

items.abstract: <jats:p>Let ω(n) be the sum of the squares of the coefficients of the product of (1 + x^(2^i+1) + x^(2^(i+1)+1)) for i = 0, ..., n-1 (OEIS A385082). Ekhad and Zeilberger posed the computation of ω(10000) as a prize problem, observing that their algorithms, which handle all of Stanley's rational cases, fail on it; Tang and Xin computed ω(10000) by a method that does not give a polynomial-time algorithm. We prove that ω(n) is asymptotically of order ρ^n n^(-κ), with ρ = (5+√17)/2 and the irrational exponent κ = (1/2)·log_2((5+√17)/9). Since D-finite sequences of integers with at most exponential growth have asymptotic expansions with rational exponents, it follows that the generating function of ω(n) is not D-finite; in particular it is neither algebraic nor rational. We determine the asymptotics up to a continuous periodic factor, ω(n) = ρ^n n^(-κ) (Φ((1/2) log_2 n) + o(1)). We also give a polynomial-time algorithm for ω(n), and show that every sequence A·2^i + c with c ≠ 0 gives a generating function that is not D-finite. Since the largest zero 2 of (x-1)(x-2) is a Pisot–Vijayaraghavan number, this shows that the PV condition in a conjecture recorded by Stanley is not sufficient for rationality as literally stated</jats:p>
title: The Ekhad–Zeilberger sequence ω(n) is not D-finite

items.abstract: <jats:p>This is the fourth installment of the five-part saga on the Umbral Transfer-Matrix method, based on Gian-Carlo Rota's seminal notion of the umbra. In this article we describe the Maple packages USAP, USAW, and  MAYLIS. USAP automatically constructs, for any specific $r$, an Umbral Scheme for enumerating, according to perimeter, the number of self-avoiding polygons with  $\leq 2r$ horizontal edges per vertical cross-section. The much more complicated USAW does the analogous thing for self-avoiding walks. Such  Umbral Schemes enable counting these classes of self-avoiding polygons and walks in polynomial time as opposed to the exponential time that is required by naive counting. Finally MAYLIS is targeted to the special case of enumerating classes of saps with at most two horizontal edges per vertical cross-section (equivalently column-convex polyominoes by perimeter), and related classes. In this computationally trivial case we can actually automatically solve the equations that were automatically generated by USAP. As an example, we give the first fully computer-generated proof of the celebrated Delest-Viennot result that the number of convex polyominoes with perimeter $2n+8$ equals $(2n+11)4^n-4(2n+1)!/n!^2$.</jats:p>
title: The Umbral Transfer-Matrix Method. IV. Counting Self-Avoiding Polygons and Walks

items.abstract: <jats:p>We prove an explicit formula for the number of $n \times n$ upper triangular matrices, over $GF(q)$,  whose square is the zero matrix. This formula was recently conjectured by Sasha Kirillov and Anna Melnikov.</jats:p>
title: The Number of Solutions of $X^2=0$ in Triangular Matrices Over $GF(q)$

items.abstract: <jats:p>In 1981, Adriano Garsia and Steve Milne found the first bijective proof of the celebrated Rogers-Ramanujan identities. To achieve this feat, they invented a versatile tool that they called the Involution Principle. In this note we revisit this useful principle from a very general perspective, independent of its application to specific combinatorial identities, and will explore its complexity.</jats:p>
title: Experimenting with the Garsia-Milne Involution Principle
